answer_text:
Let \(N\) be the number of games played.

### 1. Upper bound

Fix one student, say student \(A\).

- In each game that \(A\) participates in, \(A\) is paired with \(3\) other students.
- Since any two students can appear together **at most once**, the students who appear with \(A\) in different games must all be distinct.
- There are only \(11\) other students total, so if \(A\) plays \(t\) times, then

\[
3t \le 11.
\]

Thus

\[
t \le 3.
\]

So each student can participate in at most \(3\) games.

Therefore the total number of student-game participations is at most

\[
12 \cdot 3 = 36.
\]

But each game uses \(4\) participations, so

\[
4N \le 36
\]

and hence

\[
N \le 9.
\]

So at most \(9\) games are possible.

---

### 2. Construction showing \(9\) games are possible

Label the 12 students as

\[
A_1,A_2,A_3,\quad B_1,B_2,B_3,\quad C_1,C_2,C_3,\quad D_1,D_2,D_3.
\]

Consider the following \(9\) games:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\text{Game} & A & B & C & D\\
\hline
1 & A_1 & B_1 & C_1 & D_1\\
2 & A_1 & B_2 & C_2 & D_3\\
3 & A_1 & B_3 & C_3 & D_2\\
4 & A_2 & B_1 & C_2 & D_2\\
5 & A_2 & B_2 & C_3 & D_1\\
6 & A_2 & B_3 & C_1 & D_3\\
7 & A_3 & B_1 & C_3 & D_3\\
8 & A_3 & B_2 & C_1 & D_2\\
9 & A_3 & B_3 & C_2 & D_1
\end{array}
\]

Each game has exactly \(4\) students.

Now check the condition:

- No two students from the same group \(A,B,C,D\) ever appear together.
- For any two different groups, every possible pair of students appears exactly once. For example, the \(A\)-\(B\) pairs are

\[
A_1B_1,\ A_1B_2,\ A_1B_3,\ A_2B_1,\ A_2B_2,\ A_2B_3,\ A_3B_1,\ A_3B_2,\ A_3B_3,
\]

all distinct. The same holds for any other pair of groups.

Thus no pair of students appears together more than once, so this is a valid schedule of \(9\) games.

Since \(9\) is both an upper bound and achievable, the maximum number of games is

\[
\boxed{9}
\]
